title: Divine Provision and the Diversity of Instruction
english: To guard a city, whether it be the body or the soul, is impossible unless God co-guards it. 'Those hoping in his mercy' [Ps 33:18]; he has mercy on those fearing him, to rescue their souls from death. For this reason, 'his eyes' are 'upon those fearing him' [Ps 33:18-19] and 'those hoping in his mercy', so that he may rescue 'their souls from death' [Ps 33:19]. Death here we do not take to be the common death which the pious and the impious, the righteous and the unjust, all undergo, but it is a death of the soul which consumes the soul from the blessed life.

From this death we are turned away to avoid it; concerning this it is said: 'this soul that sins shall die' [Ezek 18:4]. And again: 'sin, when completed, brings forth death' [Gal 6:8]. And since this death follows sins, God, giving the forgiveness of sins, will rescue those who have received [grace] beforehand from the following death. And he will nourish them in famine, those fearing him and hoping in his mercy. Just as he rescues souls from death, so also he nourishes them in famine.

Indeed, such things have happened many times in history. He nourished the people of the Hebrews during a long journey in the wilderness, providing manna every day by himself. And you will find this in various instances: for example, Elijah was nourished by the widow and by the angel shown to him through bread and the jar of water. And also, while Jezebel was persecuting Elijah and all the prophets of the Lord, Obadiah, the commander of the household of King Ahab, nourished fifty men in two caves, God having prepared him for this. Indeed, he said this without neglect to Elijah when he met him: 'and your servant fearing the Lord' [1 Kings 18:3]. And he who feared the Lord nourished them because of the Lord.

If, therefore, he has restorations—these other things have happened according to history—he again nourishes those fearing his fear and hoping in his mercy, providing for them the bread of life, descending from heaven, which partakes of his flesh as 'true food' [John 6:51]. Being the savior of all, he holds them. He does not do this by a single means, but according to the circumstances: he saves in wars from external enemies, making them [victorious] and not allowing them to fall into captivity, he saves...

He saves those who are doing badly, like a pilot when we are tossed by storms in the sea of life. Furthermore, he gives to each one a spring—in which is 'a spring unto eternal life' (John 4:14)—and he is nourished even when having become in a waterless place. And, 'open your eyes and be filled with bread' (Isa 58:11).

The one having opened the eyes of the soul and having been filled by the manner of chewing the bread of the divine logos does not suffer from famine; for 'the Lord will not let the soul of the righteous starve' (Ps 34:9). Whoever is in desire for bread but is not opening his eyes to his own bread, lives in famine; for the soul has many foods from God within itself.

Our soul waits upon the Lord. This is what is said: since we have known these things, that the eyes of the Lord are watching those who fear him (Ps 33:18)—even if they have at some time been in death, he rescued them; even if they have at some time been in famine, he nourished them; even if we should at some time be in any lack, we wait knowing that we too shall enjoy these things; and our soul, if it should be in death, shall be saved. For he is a helper and a defender of us.

You see that a remainder has become a multitude: 'the Lord looked down from heaven, he saw all the sons of men' (Ps 147:9). If at any time something is being said discordantly and oppositely, observe if these things are being said about one single thing; for then an opposition occurs. But if it is being said about a church or a city or a house, they are not opposites; for the things concerning the one are said, and the things concerning the other are said.

And this you ought to know: that the saints do not offer up their prayers and thanksgivings concerning themselves alone, but concerning all things which they consider. It is not the same to say one thing that must harmonize with one, and a multitude, such as a people or a nation or a city. It is impossible for the same thing to be at once good and bad, or temperate and intemperate.

And the apostle writes to the Corinthians that they have become rich 'in every word and in all knowledge' (1 Cor 1:5). Does he not say again, 'fornication is heard among you' (1 Cor 5:1)? If he were saying these things toward one person, it would be discordant. But since the whole church is being addressed, and such and such are in the collections, he says all things, so that each one may receive help for himself. In this way, too, he charges them concerning those erring about the resurrection, and concerning the gifts, and concerning those having become idolaters.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Nature of Hope and Double Names
english: How then are these enriched with all word and knowledge? They are others about whom he was speaking. In the same way, the holy one does not speak only about himself—for he was a teacher—but about all those who have death and have fallen into famine because they neglected their own land. He does not say everything about everyone, but he says everything about others, applying each thing to each.

Since he is a help and a protector for us, because of this our soul waits for him. We know that even if we propose some good things, even if we wish to run toward the beautiful things and wish to bring them to an end, unless he himself cooperates and has mercy, we are not able to establish these things. He is a helper of the needs of which we are in need; he is a protector, throwing forward his own shield so that the adversaries may not be able to wound us.

For in him our heart shall rejoice (Ps 21:6). Others rejoice in strength, in beginning, in status, or in praises, but for us, the cause of joy is the helper and protector himself. And in his holy name we have hoped (Ps 20:9). We hoped in the one who was called upon for us. And since it seems according to the other group—I do not say those who fear the Lord are even in death—to be so, observe: we hoped in a present thing. But no one hopes in what is present, but in what is coming and expected; for 'hope is a thing not seen' (Heb 11:1).

Even if they sometimes say in the manner of a prayer, 'Hallowed be thy name' (Matt 6:9), they do not say let that which is not holy be hallowed, but let it be shown, let it appear holy. Then indeed it appears holy, when he also helps us and protects us. And when we say toward the Gospel, we say many thoughts toward this: 'Hallowed be thy name,' and this was taken to mean: since we carry it, cooperate so that we may not blaspheme it, hallow it, keep it holy in us; for it is said in imperative words. It was spoken in the optative: 'May thy name be hallowed.' And another [meaning]: since they now carry your name even to idols and to demons and to the womb—for 'God is the womb' of those—when knowledge becomes to men concerning your majesty so that they make no other god, when 'all is in all' (1 Cor 15:28) becomes, your name is hallowed being snatched away from...

May it be, Lord, your mercy upon us, just as we have hoped in you. 'May your mercy be upon us.' This prayer is sent up not because they already possess the mercy; for he did not say, 'Let your mercy be preserved,' but 'May it be, just as we have hoped in you.' For this reason we hoped in you.

Observe how, according to the proportion of faith, he gives gifts, and not to all everything, nor in the same measure, but according to the measure of the faith received; and so also here: 'just as we have hoped.' Some have hoped perfectly, and some not so, but according to a certain progress, or in another way according to an introduction. 'According to the proportion' of our faith, may your mercy be upon us, Lord; for thus we hoped.

Regarding David, when he changed his face before Abimelech (1 Sam 27:1-4), and released him, and departed. To those who read the royal histories, the present narrative is clear. How intensely David was being pursued by Saul and was about to be captured, he departed to Gath toward King Achish. It is here that Abimelech is named. The word is a double name; for double names are also found in the Scripture, such as regarding Moses' father-in-law; and Jethro is called also Reuel. And Thomas is called also Didymus. And many such double names exist; Matthew seems to name Levi in Luke (Luke 5:27). But he is not he, but Matthias who was established in place of Judas, and Levi are two double names. This is evident in the Gospel according to the Hebrews.

Therefore, it is possible both the king of Gath, Achish, and Abimelech to be said. And it is possible also to impose it otherwise; many of the kings are named by a common name and a personal name, just as all those who ruled Egypt are so named Pharaoh. And their names are found, such as Sumach, Necho, as it is a name of the office, Pharaoh, while among the Romans it is Caesar. Therefore, it is possible also this: that Achish has the name of the office, and Abimelech is his personal name. So that if he has it, the mind does not struggle. You wish, then, the one to be the name of the office, and the other the personal. This is what the grammarians say, distinguishing for the sake of the personal name; for the personal name is also spoken of as being divided; it is divided for the sake of the personal name.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Alteration of the Most High's Right Hand
english: Regarding improper usage, they say that for a man, the names of species and kinds signify a common essence as appellatives, while 'this one' or 'that one' is used as a master. It is also said that 'master' signifies something else by improper usage.

I say many times: 'isometric' corresponds to 'concordant'. To be isometric is said to be in equal measure. I say that it also means to harmonize and to be in agreement. This is an improper usage; for to harmonize and to be in agreement is said of sounds. And again, we say of those who think the same and are of one mind that they are in concord. 'Master' is indeed used of those who think the same and intend the same, namely 'thinking the same' and 'being of one mind', but 'to be in concord' is an improper usage.

Therefore, it is possible for a master to be a name not distinguished by improper usage, but by appellative use, such as Abimelech, and for a title, such as Anchos. Thus the history is clear: he saw that King Saul was positioned with military power against his one man, David, and they were armed without armor. He fled there; and since it was not safe to enter a foreign city or land—for then suspicion of spies was greatest because the city-dwellers always had war against themselves—he feigned madness and let his saliva flow and acted foolishly, beating the doors of the gate, so that he might seem to be possessed by demons. Thus, those of Anchos slandered him. He says, 'I am diminished,' he says, 'when being seized, for you seize me when I am seized?' (Psalm 34:6). And they released him and he departed.

He named such a state of affairs a 'change of countenance'; for change signifies a change of quality. Thus a change of quality happened voluntarily, not involuntarily; for it happens to change involuntarily, such as when someone, having been frightened, becomes pale, or having been struck, or from some disturbance, seems to be flushed. Thus this change happened voluntarily even unto form.

And since David is often drawn up, as has been said in the preceding sections, to the Savior, you will say that the change of the countenance of the Savior is the taking on of the form of a slave. And here it has not happened as a change from one form into another form, but a concealment of form from another apparent form; for even a change of the countenance of the turning one cannot take place. And concerning him, the Savior, it is said in one of the Psalms: 'This is the al...'

The alteration of the right hand of the Most High. The right hand of the Father—and especially according to the intention of the Psalmist—is often said to be the Savior. But having become flesh, he was altered, a curse. He endured becoming sin, so that the sinners might become the righteousness of God in him (2 Cor 5:21). Therefore, the alteration is an assumption in this way, not a change; for no one would seek a change regarding the unchangeable. If not, as someone says, it is foreign.

‘This’ then is ‘the alteration of the right hand of the Most High.’ The right hand of the Most High is unchangeable. And he became sin not by chance, but so that he might make righteousness. But sin making righteousness is not a change from non-sin to being sin; for sin makes bad people, it makes injustice. But this makes righteousness of those having it. When therefore the Word becomes flesh and takes the form of a servant (John 1:14), he was altered according to the person, not by change, as I have already often said, but by assumption. And also: ‘We have seen him, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father’ (John 1:14), signifies the glory according to his own nature. He therefore had glory fitting the flesh which was becoming to him.

‘This is the alteration of the right hand of the Most High.’ I do not say that we should speak of an alteration here which he himself received when we were saying that the assumption of the servant's form was altered, but rather ‘this is the alteration’ which he himself alters; for he himself describes the wrath, and makes the mercies effective. He says little about glorifying and praising: ‘For I will remember from the beginning of your wonders’ (Ps 77:8). ‘And I said, Now I have begun’ (Ps 77:9). I said all things darkly, that having been troubled I did not speak, that the watchmen had come upon me, but rather: ‘Now I have begun.’ I will now narrate other things after those, those following the dark things.

‘This is the alteration of the right hand of the Most High.’ Therefore he says: ‘Who is God like our God, the great?’ (Ps 86:8). ‘You made known your power among your peoples’ (Ps 86:9). Behold, this is the alteration. Then he altered his countenance. You can take the king of Egypt more allegorically as the ruler of this world, the devil. Therefore, the place which is among us is a land of different tribes. And just as when Egypt is named, it is the place upon the earth, Pharaoh is called the one ruling and tyrannizing, and when Babylon, Nebuchadnezzar is called, and when Assyria...
